name: Childhood diarrhoea
tagline: ORS saves lives. Know the signs of dehydration.

urgent.heading: Urgent — get to a clinic or hospital
urgent.primary_message: Dehydration in a small child can become fatal within hours. If you see any of these signs, don't wait. Go.
red_flags: Child very thirsty but unable to drink
Sunken eyes, dry mouth, no tears when crying
Sunken soft spot on the top of a baby's head
Very little or no urine in 6+ hours
Lethargy — child is drowsy, hard to wake, or unresponsive
Vomiting that prevents keeping any fluid down

what_is_it.heading: Childhood diarrhoea in plain terms
what_is_it.lede: Diarrhoea is loose, watery stools — three or more in 24 hours. In small children, the danger is not the diarrhoea itself. It is the dehydration that follows.
paragraphs: Children's bodies are small and they dehydrate fast. A child who has lost too much water becomes weak, then drowsy, then critical — sometimes within hours. Diarrhoea remains one of the leading causes of death in South African children under 5.

Most childhood diarrhoea is viral and resolves in 3–5 days. The main treatment is replacing lost fluids — Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS) is the gold standard. Free at every clinic. Has saved millions of children worldwide.

items.headline: Top killer
items.body: Diarrhoeal disease remains one of the leading killers of SA children under 5 — almost always from dehydration.

items.headline: ORS saves lives
items.body: Oral Rehydration Solution prevents and treats most dehydration. Free at every clinic. Cheap, simple, effective.

items.headline: Rotavirus vaccine
items.body: Free SA childhood vaccine prevents the most common cause of severe diarrhoea. Given at 6 weeks and 14 weeks. Don't skip.

items.headline: No antibiotics
items.body: Most diarrhoea is viral. Antibiotics don't help — and can make some kinds worse. Don't ask for them; ask for ORS.

pull_quote.text: A child can have hundreds of millilitres of diarrhoea in a day. Every 250ml of stool lost needs to be replaced with 250ml of ORS — or more. Keep the cup ready.

signs.heading: How to spot dehydration
signs.lede: Dehydration develops in stages. Catching it at the 'thirsty' stage keeps the child out of hospital.

items.title: Mild — treatable at home
items.description: Child is thirsty, drinks eagerly, slightly less playful, urine slightly darker but still wet nappies. Give ORS, breastmilk, or clean water.

items.title: Moderate — go to clinic
items.description: Child very thirsty, dry mouth, fewer wet nappies, restless or irritable, sunken eyes, skin slow to bounce back when pinched. Clinic — not hospital yet.

items.title: Severe — hospital now
items.description: Child too weak to drink, drowsy or unresponsive, no tears, no wet nappy for 6+ hours, sunken soft spot in a baby. This is an emergency.

spreads.heading: How childhood diarrhoea spreads
yes: Faecal-oral route — tiny amounts of stool getting onto food, hands, or water
Contaminated water in areas without safe supply
Unwashed hands after toilet or nappy changes
Sharing toys, dummies, or bottles in childcare settings
Food that has gone off or wasn't cooked thoroughly
no: Breastfeeding — breastmilk actually protects against diarrhoea
Eating slightly spicy food (in older children)

prevention.heading: How to protect your child
prevention.lede: Most childhood diarrhoea is preventable with vaccines, clean water, and good handwashing. Worth the small daily effort.

items.title: Rotavirus vaccine
items.description: Free SA childhood vaccine at 6 weeks and 14 weeks. Prevents the most common cause of severe childhood diarrhoea. Never skip it.

items.title: Clean hands, clean water
items.description: Wash hands with soap before food, after toilet, after nappy changes. Use safe water for drinking and cooking. Boil if unsure.

items.title: Breastfeed if you can
items.description: Breastmilk contains antibodies that protect against diarrhoea. Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months is one of the strongest protections.

items.title: Food safety
items.description: Cook meat fully, refrigerate leftovers promptly, wash fruit and vegetables. Don't give very young children unpasteurised milk or undercooked eggs.

items.title: Start ORS at the first loose stool
items.description: Mix one sachet in 1 litre of clean water (or as packet says). Give frequent small sips after every loose stool — 50–100ml for under-2s, 100–200ml for older children.

items.title: Keep breastfeeding or formula going
items.description: Don't stop breastfeeding during diarrhoea — breastmilk is protective. Keep formula going. Babies need normal feeds plus extra ORS.

items.title: Give zinc supplements
items.description: Free at clinics together with ORS. Zinc shortens diarrhoea by 25% and reduces severity. Give for 10–14 days as advised.

items.title: Watch for dehydration signs
items.description: Check wet nappies, tears when crying, alertness. Pinch the skin on the tummy gently — it should bounce back fast. If anything seems off, go to clinic.

items.title: Go to clinic or hospital if it worsens
items.description: Moderate dehydration — clinic. Severe dehydration — hospital. Don't second-guess. The treatment (IV fluids) is fast and life-saving.

get_help.heading: Where to go
get_help.lede: Childhood diarrhoea care is one of South Africa's strongest public health systems. Free ORS, free vaccines, free hospital care if needed. Use it early.
